messages.subject: fitqtl, get.ests for binary data
parts:
Hello Karl,

I am struggling to interpret the estimated QTL effects from fitqtl. I am working with binary data from an intercross, and as I understand it, this means the intercept and estimated effects should all be between -1 and 1 (correct?). I ran the fitqtl with both hk and imp methods to compare the results, but both methods gave results that seem very strange:


Haley Knott method:

out.fq3_2 <- fitqtl(dat, pheno.col=2, qtl=qtl.multi3, formula=y~Q1*Q2+Q3+Q4, method="hk", model="binary", dropone=FALSE, get.ests=TRUE)

summary(out.fq3_2)


fitqtl summary

Method: Haley-Knott regression
Model: binary phenotype
Number of observations : 340

Full model result
----------------------------------
Model formula: y ~ Q1 + Q2 + Q3 + Q4 + Q1:Q2

df LOD %var Pvalue(Chi2)
Model 12 70.78629 61.66371 0


Estimated effects:

est SE t

1...@65.0d:1...@151.0a 2.78107 0.78773 3.530
1...@65.0a:1...@151.0d -0.36652 0.71973 -0.509
1...@65.0d:1...@151.0d 1.15873 1.01266 1.144




Multiple imputations method:

out.fq4_2 <- fitqtl(datdraws256, pheno.col=2, qtl=qtl.multi4, formula=y~Q1*Q2+Q3+Q4, method="imp", model="binary", dropone=FALSE, get.ests=TRUE)

summary(out.fq4_2)


fitqtl summary

Model: binary phenotype
Number of observations : 340

Full model result
----------------------------------

df LOD %var Pvalue(Chi2)
Model 12 69.10353 60.7799 0


Estimated effects:
-----------------
est SE t
Intercept -3.43235 24.39745 -0.141
1...@65.0a -0.10963 0.42961 -0.255
1...@65.0d -0.60001 1.35551 -0.443
1...@151.0a -0.08361 0.81379 -0.103
1...@151.0d 0.60693 1.30778 0.464
3...@157.0a 7.33318 46.76674 0.157
3...@157.0d 2.97599 44.36301 0.067
9...@102.0a 0.77060 0.49171 1.567
9...@102.0d 0.83353 0.44677 1.866
1...@65.0a:1...@151.0a -0.32894 0.50099 -0.657
1...@65.0d:1...@151.0a 2.28163 1.65532 1.378
1...@65.0a:1...@151.0d -0.61879 1.14387 -0.541
1...@65.0d:1...@151.0d 0.78477 4.29312 0.183



I don't understand why the est values are so high for some QTL, how the SE value could be higher than the est value, and why the results are so different between the hk and imp methods.

Does this mean there is something fundamentally wrong with how I am running this analysis? Any idea what I might be missing?


Thank you very much for your help.

Best regards,
Maridel

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] fitqtl, get.ests for binary data
parts:
With model=“binary”, fitqtl is using a logistic regression model. 
See for example https://stats.idre.ucla.edu/other/mult-pkg/faq/general/faq-how-do-i-interpret-odds-ratios-in-logistic-regression/

karl
